'''''Digitaria sanguinalis''''' is a species of [[Poaceae|grass]] known by several [[common name]]s, including '''hairy crabgrass''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=DISA|taxon=Digitaria sanguinalis|accessdate=18 January 2016}}</ref> '''hairy finger-grass''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref> '''large crabgrass''', '''crab finger grass''', '''purple crabgrass'''.<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | accessdate=6 February 2015}}</ref> It is one of the better-known species of the genus ''[[Digitaria]]'', and one that is known nearly worldwide as a common weed. It is used as animal fodder, and the seeds are edible and have been used as a grain in Germany and especially Poland, where it is sometimes cultivated.<ref>Georgia, Ada E. 1914. [http://chestofbooks.com/flora-plants/weeds/Manual-Of-Weeds/index.html A Manual of Weeds]. The Macmillan Company. [http://chestofbooks.com/flora-plants/weeds/Manual-Of-Weeds/Crab-Grass-Digitaria-sanguinalis-Scop-Syntherisma-sangui.html ''Digitaria sanguinalis'' section]</ref>  This has earned it the name Polish millet.<ref>[http://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/polish%20millet Polish millet - Merriam-Webster Online]{{subscription required}}</ref>

==Description==
It is an annual grass with an [[inflorescence]] of up to nine very long, very thin, radiating branches atop its stems. Each branch is lined with pairs of very tiny [[raceme|spikelets]]. The inflorescences may be reddish or purplish.

==Uses==
During the European [[Middle Ages]], ''Digitaria sanguinalis'' was cultivated by [[Slavic peoples|Slavic]] peoples in [[Eastern Europe]], where it was cooked in soups and porridges.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Nesbitt |first1=Mark |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=47 |isbn=0415927463}}</ref>

The plant was brought to the United States by immigrants to serve as hand-foraged grain.  The grass is also highly nutritious, especially before the plant exhausts itself producing seed.  It is frequently sown in fields to provide graze for animals, or clipped and bundled as [[hay]]. Compared to other grasses, it has a relatively high protein percentage.<ref>{{PFAF}}</ref>  Farmers will sometimes till patches in their pastures in the late spring, with the intent of encouraging crabgrass seed.

For human consumption, crabgrass necessarily must be harvested by hand, because it produces grain throughout summer, rather than simultaneously.  Machine harvesting would require monthly passes, and even then much of the seed would go to waste. Crabgrass produces an exceptionally high amount of grain, it smothers other weeds, it acts as its own mulch, and it can survive both heat and drought.  Its adaptability makes it a candidate for environmental small-farming.<ref name= Deane >{{cite web |url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/crabgrass-digitaria-sanguinalis-2/ |title=Crabgrass Was King |author=Green Deane}}</ref>

==Control==
Its usefulness to nineteenth-century homesteaders has made its seed widespread, and today is generally considered an unattractive nuisance. Crabgrass takes advantage of low fertility and drought, since this tends to weaken other grasses and it tends to invade [[Lawn|manicured turf]]. It is difficult to kill, as it will regenerate, and chemicals will likely harm surrounding grasses.  As an [[Annual plant|annual]], it can be controlled by [[preemergent herbicides]].  The most efficient means of control is to pull patches, and keep the rest of the lawn watered and mowed at a height of two to three inches.<ref>[http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/18916 ''Digitaria sanguinalis'' - Cabi]</ref>
